questions.q: Adding one more electron to a large piece of metal costs almost no energy. Why does adding one to a tiny island cost a lot?
options: A tiny island has a tiny capacitance, and the charging energy e²/2C grows as the capacitance shrinks
A tiny island has fewer atoms, so each electron must be squeezed between them with force
A tiny island is always colder, so electrons need extra energy to move onto it
A tiny island is made of an insulator, which resists every extra electron
questions.explain: Charge comes in whole electrons, and the cost of one more is the charging energy e²/2C. A smaller island has a smaller capacitance C, so the cost rises: tens to hundreds of meV on a nanometre island.

questions.q: The graph shows the cost of adding one electron to an island against its diameter, with the thermal energy at three temperatures. Roughly how small must an island be for single-electron effects to work at room temperature?
questions.alt: Energy on a log scale against island diameter from 1 nm to 1000 nm: the cost of adding one electron falls from about 400 meV at 1 nm to under 1 meV at 1000 nm; dashed lines mark the thermal energy at 300 K, 77 K and 4.2 K
options: About 1–2 nm, so that the cost is about ten times the thermal energy
About 100 nm, the size of a large virus
About 1 µm, the size that already works at 4.2 K
Any size, because the cost does not depend on the island's size
questions.explain: At 300 K the thermal energy is about 26 meV. A clean blockade needs a charging energy about ten times that, which means islands of only 1–2 nm. Larger islands work only when cold: below about 1 K for a micrometre.

questions.q: Coulomb blockade needs a charging energy well above the thermal energy. What is its second condition?
options: The tunnel junctions must have a high resistance (above about 26 kΩ), so each electron really sits on the island
The island must hold at least 100 electrons, so that its charge is smooth
The island must be made of a superconductor, so that the electrons pair up
The island must be lit by a laser, which gives the electrons the energy to tunnel
questions.explain: The junctions must be 'opaque': more than about h/e² ≈ 26 kΩ each, so that every electron spends long enough on the island for the charging energy to count.

questions.q: In a single-electron transistor (SET), what takes the place of a MOSFET's channel?
options: A tiny island between two tunnel junctions, with a gate close by
A quantum well between two thin walls, with no gate at all
A single carbon nanotube joined directly to the source and drain
A thin superconducting wire between the source and drain
questions.explain: An SET is like a MOSFET whose channel is replaced by a tiny island between two tunnel junctions. The gate sits close to the island but no electrons cross to it: it only changes the island's energy.

questions.q: In a blocked SET, how does raising the gate voltage let current flow?
options: It lowers the island's energy levels until one sits between the source and drain, so electrons pass one at a time
It raises the source's energy until it is above every level on the island
It removes the charging energy, so the island behaves like a large piece of metal
It thins the tunnel junctions until electrons can pass straight from source to drain
questions.explain: The island's energy levels form a ladder, one charging energy apart. The gate lowers the ladder until an empty level sits between the source and drain: electrons then hop on and off one at a time.

questions.q: True or false: as the gate voltage of an SET rises steadily, each peak in the current corresponds to one more electron being added to the island.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. The current switches on and off again and again, one peak per extra electron. The peaks are evenly spaced because each extra electron needs the same extra charge on the gate.

questions.q: The graph shows the current of an SET against gate voltage at three temperatures. What happens to the peaks as the island gets warmer?
questions.alt: Current against gate voltage at three temperatures: cold, warmer and hot
options: They broaden and blur together, because thermal kicks let electrons through between the peaks
They get sharper and taller, because warm electrons move faster
They move closer together, because each electron needs less gate voltage
They stay exactly the same, because the charging energy does not depend on temperature
questions.explain: Heat gives electrons random kicks of about k_BT. When this approaches the charging energy, electrons get through between the peaks, which blur together: at 40% of the charging energy they have almost gone.

questions.q: The map shows the current of an SET as both the gate voltage and the source–drain voltage are changed. What is true inside each white diamond?
questions.alt: A colour map of current against gate voltage (across) and source–drain voltage (up): white diamond shapes sit along the zero line, surrounded by blue current
options: No current flows, and the island holds a fixed number of electrons
The current is at its largest, and the island is empty
Electrons pass in pairs, as in a superconductor
The island is too hot for single-electron effects to show
questions.explain: Inside each white 'Coulomb diamond' the current is blocked and the island holds a fixed number of electrons (0, 1, 2 …). The diamond's height measures the island's capacitance.

questions.q: What are single-electron devices actually good for today?
options: As ultra-sensitive charge detectors, and as pumps that define the ampere
As the main switches in low-power processors
As the memory cells in smartphones and laptops
As the amplifiers in mobile-phone radios
questions.explain: An SET biased halfway up a peak is the most sensitive charge detector known, used to read spin qubits. A single-electron pump moves exactly one electron per cycle, I = ef, which helps realise the ampere.

questions.q: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis. What did their 1984–85 experiment show?
options: A whole superconducting circuit can tunnel and has quantised energy levels: the basis of today's qubits
Single electrons can be counted one at a time as they tunnel through a junction
Light can tunnel through a thin gap between two glass blocks
Electrons can tunnel through a 1 nm insulating layer between two magnets
questions.explain: They biased a Josephson junction and found that, at the lowest temperatures, the whole circuit still escaped its energy dip by tunnelling, and that microwaves revealed quantised levels. Circuits like this are the qubits of Google's and IBM's quantum processors.
